title: Asking What a Director Sees Can Change What Vision-Language Models Choose

problem.summary: Because the ability is this important, its reported failures matter.
statements: Because the ability is this important, its reported failures matter.

Many tests ask for the report and the action in one prompt: the model states what the other person can see or know, then predicts what that person will do, or acts for them (Gu et al., 2026; Juneja et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026).
When the report is right and the action is wrong, the pair is read as a failure to use the perspective: the model can see the other's view but does not work from it.

Benchmarks test level1 visual perspective-taking, judging what another person can see, and level-2, judging how it looks to them (Flavell et al., 1981), in vision-language models (Gao et al., 2025; Góral et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Linsley et al., 2025).

components: A director and a participant sit on two sides of a grid of slots, some blocked from the director's view, and the procedure makes clear that only objects both of them can see are part of the game (Keysar et al., 2000).

When the director asks for "the small candle" and the smallest candle stands in a blocked slot, reaching for that candle is scored as an egocentric error, and adults still make it (Keysar et al., 2000, 2003).
The verdict rests on an assumption that the standard protocol never checks: asking for the report leaves the action unchanged.
